summary:
The United Arab Emirates screens gender identity against travel documents at entry. In 2025 two Israeli trans women were held for hours at Dubai airport, subjected to X-ray examination to compare their genitals with the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, denied entry and had their passports confiscated.

Refusals span at least a decade. In March 2022 Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before an Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman. In August 2016 trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport with her passport confiscated after authorities declined to recognise her gender as legitimate.

The legal framework explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles. Transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law, Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, with a minimum of six months imprisonment and no maximum prescribed. The same provision also criminalises extra-marital heterosexual intercourse.

Cross-dressing liability now centres on access to sex-segregated space. Under Article 412(2) men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space face up to one year imprisonment and a fine of up to AED 10,000. This replaced a broader prior ban on wearing clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances.

There is no legal gender recognition. No protection exists under any United Arab Emirates law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Trans-specific enforcement is documented. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women who called Dubai police about prejudice witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for imitating women, held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. On 9 August 2017 two Singaporean nationals were convicted in Abu Dhabi and sentenced to one year in prison for attempting to resemble women, then deported on 28 August after nearly three weeks in custody including time in a cell described as designated for effeminate people.

A Brazilian trans woman detained since September 2022 after refusing a police-requested toxicology test remained in prolonged custody in the United Arab Emirates and accused the consulate of negligence in April 2023.

Detention carries documented risk of mistreatment connected to suspected or established same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture. Detainees have been held in cells designated for effeminate people. Involuntary medical and psychological measures, including administration of hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatment, have occurred.

Broader enforcement illustrates how public decency provisions are used. Cases include six-month sentences plus deportation for two Indian men in 2012 for consensual sex in a public bus-station toilet, three-year sentences plus deportation for a British man and another man in 2012 for drunken public sex, a one-year sentence plus deportation for a Belgian man in June 2012 after admitting a homosexual relationship with a Filipino man, a police raid breaking up a gathering of 30 men in Dubai on 21 March 2012, and a 2005 Abu Dhabi raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding that resulted in twelve convictions with eleven five-year sentences and one one-year sentence and initial reports that some men were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences.

Seeking police help has exposed complainants to criminal suspicion. In July 2007 in Dubai a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy who was kidnapped and raped was initially treated by police as a suspect. Fear of charge under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country. No formal charges were brought against him and he later received AED 15 million in civil compensation. A 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused the authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. In October 2017 a Scottish tourist arrested for public indecency after touching a man's hip had charges dropped only after intervention by Dubai ruler Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.

Officials have publicly declared there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the United Arab Emirates.
tangentialFactors:
Censorship restricts access to information on sexual orientation and gender identity. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word gay or sex.

The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a Protect Trans Lives transgender flag.

In 2022 the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word mithli. In June 2023 Amazon blocked 150 search terms including lgbtq, pride and closeted gay on its United Arab Emirates site under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist.

In June 2023 the band Steps refused a Dubai show over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.
localsOnly:
Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances.

LGBTI organisations cannot register. No LGBTQI support or advocacy organisations operate openly anywhere in the country, and in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs exist. A nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent establishment of such organisations or community education.

Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation.

Prosecution under Article 409(5) may be brought only upon complaint by a spouse or guardian, who may withdraw it at any time to terminate proceedings or suspend an imposed penalty. Because same-sex marriage is not recognised and civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible, while prosecution of female-female conduct remains possible where a husband as spouse or a father or male relative as guardian under the Islamic wali concept exists.

Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021 came into force on 2 January 2022, replacing the 1987 Federal Penal Code. A 2020 amendment had removed stoning and flogging as prescribed punishments. The 2021 law does not prescribe the death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct. The death penalty for sexual offences applies exclusively to non-consensual acts such as rape of a minor or rape resulting in death. There has never been a documented case of the death penalty applied for homosexual activity, and all documented stoning sentences involved heterosexual adultery and were commuted or overturned.

There have been no known arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex sexual activity since at least 2015 as of 2026, consistent with United States Department of State annual human rights reports after 2015 recording no cases and its 2022 report stating no known reports of arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources is whether X-ray and genital verification at airports reflects written procedure or discretionary practice by border officers, and how consistently it is applied across ports of entry.

Not sourced is how the Article 409 complaint requirement operates in practice for foreign visitors without a local spouse or guardian present, particularly given continued public decency prosecutions for related conduct.

Not sourced is the current enforcement boundary of Article 412(2) outside women-only spaces and whether appearance alone continues to prompt police action under other public decency provisions.
